advisory.checklist_item: - [ ] Free or share per-commit snapmaps once no remaining commit will use that commit as its first parent, so memory does not grow with commits times SNAPSHOTs
evidence: src/rebar/_commands/reclaim_collapse.py:520: snapmap = dict(self.snapmaps[first])
src/rebar/_commands/reclaim_collapse.py:543: self.snapmaps[new] = snapmap
src/rebar/_commands/reclaim_collapse.py:441: self.snapmaps: dict[str, dict[bytes, tuple[str, str]]] = {}
No code ever deletes entries from self.snapmaps, source_of or k_of, even after no later commit can use that commit as a first parent.
src/rebar/_commands/reclaim_collapse.py:523: for path, (mode, oid) in snapmap.items():
src/rebar/_commands/reclaim_collapse.py:441: self.snapmaps: dict[str, dict[bytes, tuple[str, str]]] = {}  (nothing ever removes entries from it)

The commit message targets 13,119 replayed commits; reclaim_collapse_stream.py's docstring describes a tree of about 221k files. With thousands of SNAPSHOT files, that means tens to hundreds of millions of retained dict entries.
advisory.finding: _StreamedRewrite keeps a full copy of the SNAPSHOT path map for every commit it writes and never frees any of them. Memory therefore grows with the number of replayed commits times the number of SNAPSHOT files. On the real store (13,119 commits and a tree of about 221k files) that can be very large, which undercuts the goal of this change: making a real-size collapse workable.
merged_from: `_StreamedRewrite._replay` makes a full copy of the first parent's SNAPSHOT path map (path to mode and blob id) for every replayed commit and keeps every copy in `self.snapmaps` until the run ends. Memory and copy time are therefore O(replayed commits × SNAPSHOT files in the tree), even though in a mostly linear history only the current tip's map (plus any pending merge parents) is ever read again. The loop over the map at line 523 also scans every SNAPSHOT path on every commit, so time is O(N×S) as well.
scenarios: Real tickets branch: 13k replayed commits, each keeping a copy of a map with thousands of SNAPSHOT entries.
advisory.suggested_fix: Before the loop, count how many remaining commits will use each commit as their first parent (from the rev-list --parents output). Drop a commit's snapmaps, source_of and k_of entries once its count reaches zero, or let a child take over its parent's map in place when it is that parent's only child.

advisory.checklist_item: - [ ] Catch OSError/BrokenPipeError in ObjectReader.read/close and re-raise as StreamError, and raise StreamError when read(size) returns fewer than size bytes
evidence: src/rebar/_commands/reclaim_collapse_stream.py:173: stdin.write(oid.encode() + b"\n")
src/rebar/_commands/reclaim_collapse_stream.py:180: body = stdout.read(size)
src/rebar/_commands/reclaim_collapse_stream.py:181: stdout.read(1)  # trailing newline
src/rebar/_commands/reclaim_collapse_stream.py:186: self._proc.stdin.close()
src/rebar/_commands/reclaim_collapse.py:151: except (ReclaimCollapseError, ShadowSafetyError, subprocess.CalledProcessError) as exc:
src/rebar/_commands/reclaim_collapse.py:107-108: finally: rewrite.close_reader()
advisory.finding: ObjectReader does not turn pipe failures into StreamError. If git cat-file --batch exits, stdin.write/flush raises a raw BrokenPipeError, and BrokenPipeError is not in the cli() except tuple, so the CLI fails with a traceback instead of a reclaim-collapse error. Also, stdout.read(size) is never checked for a short read, so a truncated object body can be cached and used as if it were complete. close_reader() runs in a finally block, so a BrokenPipeError raised while closing can hide the original exception.
scenarios: cat-file is killed or crashes partway through the run: the write raises BrokenPipeError, which escapes as a traceback.
cat-file closes stdout partway through a body: read(size) returns fewer bytes, which are cached as the full object, and json.loads may then treat a real SNAPSHOT as a non-SNAPSHOT.
advisory.suggested_fix: Wrap the write, flush and reads in try/except (BrokenPipeError, OSError) and raise StreamError from them. Raise StreamError if len(body) != size or if the trailing byte is not b"\n". In close(), suppress BrokenPipeError and check the returncode.

advisory.checklist_item: - [ ] Assert each replayed commit's full rewritten parent list (in-range parents map through old_to_new; out-of-range parents map to the expected anchor or tip) and that `ledger_anchor_sha` is reachable from `rewritten_tip`, rather than comparing parent counts only
evidence: tests/unit/test_reclaim_collapse.py:642: `assert len(new_parents) == len(old_parents)`: only the count is compared
tests/unit/test_reclaim_collapse.py:668: the only parent-identity check is `split()[1] == side_new` on the merge

src/rebar/_commands/reclaim_collapse.py:510-521: added parent mapping (`mapped = self.old_to_new.get(parent)` / `if mapped is None and parent not in in_range: mapped = self.current_tip`) followed by `self._diff_lines(self.source_of[first], commit, snapmap)`, which makes the tree right whatever `first` is

src/rebar/_commands/reclaim_collapse.py:483: `self._map(boundary, self.checkpoint_sha)`, so a commit whose original parent is the boundary is attached to the checkpoint, not the ledger anchor. Nothing asserts which of the two is intended, or that `result.enforce_since`/`ledger_anchor_sha` is reachable from `rewritten_tip`
advisory.finding: The oracle test never checks which commit each rewritten parent points to. It checks only the parent count and the merge's second parent. The new `_replay` builds each commit's tree from a diff against `source_of[first]`, so a commit attached to the wrong first parent still gets the correct tree, and every other assertion in the test still passes. The test therefore cannot catch a wrong mapping in the new parent-building code.
scenarios: Named input: in `_build_branchy_store`, commit 's: delete' has the boundary as its original parent. The test passes whether its rewritten first parent is `checkpoint_sha`, `ledger_anchor_sha` or any other written commit, because its tree is diffed against `source_of[first]`, which is the boundary either way.
If 's: side event and snapshot' is attached to the wrong first parent, every assertion except the merge's second-parent check still passes.
advisory.suggested_fix: In the oracle loop, for each in-range original parent `p`, assert `old_to_new[p]` is in `new_parents` at the same index. For parents that are not in range (or are the boundary), assert the expected written commit explicitly. Also add `git merge-base --is-ancestor result.ledger_anchor_sha result.rewritten_tip` with an asserted exit code.

advisory.checklist_item: - [ ] Assert an exact `result.ledger_entries_rewritten` in the branchy oracle test, where a rewritten SNAPSHOT is carried through replayed commits, so the new write-only counting is pinned
evidence: tests/unit/test_reclaim_collapse.py:274: `_set_horizon_ref(tracker, boundary)`, so the range boundary..tip is empty and no commits are replayed
tests/unit/test_reclaim_collapse.py:282: `assert result.ledger_entries_rewritten == 1`, the same value under both counting rules

src/rebar/_commands/reclaim_collapse.py:524-528: added `if path not in changed and self._latest(oid) <= k_first: continue` ... `self.ledger_rewrites += count`, which is the code behind the new counting
Absence: neither `test_streamed_engine_matches_the_rewrite_oracle` nor `test_streamed_engine_runs_one_fast_import_and_one_batch_reader` asserts `ledger_entries_rewritten`
advisory.finding: The commit message and the CollapseResult docstring say `ledger_entries_rewritten` now counts only SNAPSHOT blobs actually written, so a SNAPSHOT carried unchanged into later commits is not counted again. No test pins this. The one existing assertion uses a store with zero replayed commits, where the old and new counting both give 1.
scenarios: Named input: `_build_branchy_store`. The below-boundary SNAPSHOT `101-a2222222-...-SNAPSHOT.json` is rewritten at the ledger anchor and carried unchanged through the replayed commits. The old writer counted it again in every replayed commit; the new writer should count it once. No assertion tells the two apart, so a regression back to per-commit counting, or a skip that drops a needed rewrite, would go unnoticed.
advisory.suggested_fix: In `test_streamed_engine_matches_the_rewrite_oracle`, assert `result.ledger_entries_rewritten == N`, where N counts the anchor rewrite of the fork SNAPSHOT, the retired SNAPSHOT's rewrite, and the merge's re-resolution of the side SNAPSHOT, each counted once.

advisory.checklist_item: - [ ] Bound the total subprocess count in the one-fast-import test (e.g. `len(spawned) <= replayed + C`, and at most one `ls-tree`) instead of only forbidding the two old call shapes
evidence: tests/unit/test_reclaim_collapse.py:734: `assert not [args for args in git_calls if args[:2] == ("cat-file", "blob")]`
tests/unit/test_reclaim_collapse.py:735: `assert not [args for args in git_calls if args and args[0] == "fast-import"]`

The `spawned` list (line 712) already records every Popen, since `stream.subprocess` is the global subprocess module, but the test only checks it for 'fast-import' and '--batch'
advisory.finding: The subprocess-count test is meant to guard against the per-commit and per-blob subprocess blow-up, but it only forbids the two exact old call shapes (`_git('cat-file','blob',...)` and `_git('fast-import',...)`). It sets no limit on other per-commit or per-blob git calls, so bringing back a full `ls-tree` on every replayed commit would still pass. It also depends on the private `engine._git` name.
scenarios: Named input: the 50-commit, 200-file fixture. If `_replay` were changed to call `self._snapshot_paths(commit)`, which runs `ls-tree -rz`, per commit, or to read blobs through `_git("cat-file", "-p", oid)`, all four assertions would still pass.
advisory.suggested_fix: Add `assert sum(1 for a in git_calls if a and a[0] == "ls-tree") <= 1` and `assert len(spawned) <= result.replayed_commits + 20` (or a similar linear bound), so any per-blob or per-commit full-tree process shows up.

advisory.finding: The stream-failure test accepts any `ReclaimCollapseError` (no `match=`). The fault fires at the second commit, and the scratch-ref absence check likely holds even without the new cleanup, because fast-import probably only writes refs when the stream finishes. So the added `_delete_ref` in the `except StreamError` branch, and a failure in the middle of replay, are not shown to work.
scenarios: Named sequence: remove the `_delete_ref` call at line 105. The ref likely still never exists because fast-import died before updating refs, so the line-749 check still passes.
If `StreamError` stopped being converted (e.g. the error came from `_raw_commit` instead of the stream), `pytest.raises` without `match` would still pass.
advisory.suggested_fix: Use `pytest.raises(engine.ReclaimCollapseError, match="git fast-import")`. Add a second case where the failure happens at a replayed commit (e.g. monkeypatch `FastImportSession.commit` to raise `StreamError` on its third call), and assert HEAD and the scratch refs are unchanged.

advisory.checklist_item: - [ ] Stop caching every object in ObjectReader forever: skip caching commit objects and bound or evict the blob cache (refs_of already holds the parsed refs).
evidence: src/rebar/_commands/reclaim_collapse_stream.py:164: self._cache: dict[str, bytes] = {}
src/rebar/_commands/reclaim_collapse_stream.py:182: self._cache[oid] = body
reclaim_collapse.py `_raw_commit`: raw = self.reader.read(commit) is called once per replayed commit, so caching commit bodies is never reused
reclaim_collapse.py `_refs` already caches the parsed ledger refs per oid in self.refs_of; only `_rewritten` re-reads the blob bytes
advisory.finding: `ObjectReader.read` keeps every object body it fetches in `self._cache` for the life of the run, and never evicts anything. That includes every replayed commit object, which is read exactly once by `_raw_commit`, and every distinct SNAPSHOT-candidate blob across the whole history. The parsed result each SNAPSHOT is actually needed for is already cached separately in `refs_of`, so these retained raw bodies are mostly dead weight.
scenarios: Collapsing a long history in which SNAPSHOTs are rewritten many times: every SNAPSHOT version ever introduced above the boundary, plus every SNAPSHOT at the boundary, stays in memory
advisory.suggested_fix: Add a `cache` flag to `ObjectReader.read` and pass False from `_raw_commit`, or replace the dict with a bounded LRU cache. Only `_rewritten` re-reads blob bytes, and it can afford a cache miss.
